description: SHA-512 outer-length falls to default=SHA-384 constant

findings.title: SHA-512 HMAC outer-round length is computed as 384 bits
findings.description: In hmac_core__always_comb__assign_sha_message_length__001 (hmac_core.sv lines 221-229 of the shown fragment), the final-hash branch only has explicit cases for SHA2_256 and SHA2_384. SHA2_512 falls into the `default` arm, which sets `sha_msg_len = BlockSizeSHA512in64 + 64'd384` instead of `+ 64'd512`. As a result, when SHA-512 HMAC is used, the core believes the outer message is 128 bits shorter than it really is. The StMsg logic in hmac_core__always_comb__next_state__001 (lines around 355-367 of the shown fragment) uses `txcount >= sha_message_length_o` to stop reading data and assert processing, so the outer hash can be finalized before the full 512-bit inner digest has been consumed.
findings.security_impact: SHA-512 HMAC results become non-standard/incorrect. Any security function relying on SHA-512 HMAC can fail authentication or integrity checks, causing denial of service and protocol failure.

findings.title: Active HMAC operation uses mutable digest_size instead of the started digest size
findings.description: The design clearly distinguishes between the configured digest size and the digest size latched when an operation started: hmac__always_comb__assign_digest_reg__001 (hmac.sv lines 260-283 of the shown fragment) uses `digest_size_started_q` for digest HW->SW handling. However, the logic that feeds the inner digest into the outer HMAC round still uses the live configuration. In hmac__always_comb__select_fifo_wdata__001 (hmac.sv lines 554-561), the number/format of digest words written to the FIFO is selected from current `digest_size`, not `digest_size_started_q`. In hmac_core__always_comb__next_state__001 (lines around 398-411), StPushToMsgFifo also decides the terminal word count from current `digest_size_i`. If software changes digest size after start but before/during the outer round, the core can truncate a SHA-512 inner digest to 256/384 bits, reinterpret a SHA-256 digest as 512-bit data, or even fail to hit any valid termination condition for an unsupported value and hang in the push state.
findings.security_impact: Software that can rewrite control registers during an active hash can corrupt or stall HMAC computations, undermining integrity checks and potentially causing denial of service.

description: wipe/cfg_block protocol: cfg_block clears on stop before done

findings.title: cfg_block is cleared on hash_stop, allowing key/config changes before hashing is actually done
findings.description: In hmac.sv lines 365-373, `cfg_block` is deasserted on `reg_hash_stop` as well as `reg_hash_done`. However, `reg_hash_stop` is a stop/finalize request, not completion; completion is separately indicated by `reg_hash_done`. Because both `update_secret_key` (hmac.sv lines 214-227) and the `cfg_reg` update logic (hmac.sv lines 375-411) allow writes whenever `!cfg_block`, software can modify `secret_key` and configuration immediately after issuing STOP but before the digest operation has finished. This creates a mid-finalization mutation window where the active hash/HMAC can observe a mixed old/new key or configuration. The assertion region around hmac.sv lines 947-966 also indicates the intended invariant is that configuration must not change while processing is still initiated/in-process, so clearing `cfg_block` on STOP violates that intent.
findings.security_impact: An attacker able to issue register writes during finalization can corrupt the authenticated digest, cause computation under a partially changed secret/configuration, or bypass assumptions that the key and mode remain stable for the entire operation.

findings.title: Illegal SHA-256 + 1024-bit key configuration silently zeroes HMAC pads
findings.description: In hmac_core.sv lines 173-180 (`Key_1024` case in `adjust_key_pad_length`), the SHA-256 pads are forced to zero: `i_pad_256 = '{default: '0};` and `o_pad_256 = '{default: '0};`, with only a comment saying this combination is 'not allowed'. But the configuration register capture in hmac.sv lines 375-411 does not validate or reject an invalid `key_length`/digest-size combination before passing it into the core. As a result, if software programs `key_length = Key_1024` while using SHA-256, the engine proceeds with zeroed inner/outer pads instead of rejecting the request. The resulting HMAC computation is no longer keyed by the programmed secret in the normal way and produces an invalid, predictable authentication result.
findings.security_impact: This can effectively disable the secret-key contribution for that configuration, leading to trivially wrong or forgeable MACs if the invalid mode is selected.

findings.title: CFG writes are ignored unless the hmac_en field's write-enable fires
findings.description: In hmac.sv lines 375-411, the whole cached configuration register is updated only when `!cfg_block && reg2hw.cfg.hmac_en.qe` is true, and then `cfg_reg <= reg2hw.cfg;` copies all fields. This means writes that modify only other fields of the CFG register (for example `sha_en`, `endian_swap`, `digest_swap`, `key_swap`, `digest_size`, or `key_length`) without asserting `hmac_en.qe` are silently dropped. On buses that support partial/byte writes, software can believe it changed the hashing mode or key handling while hardware continues using stale settings.
findings.security_impact: Silent retention of stale digest-size, endian, or key-length settings can cause authentication to run in a different mode than intended, producing incorrect digests and potentially undermining protocol/security assumptions.

description: Stale completion: 127-cycle cool_down delay before hash_done_event

findings.title: Stop command can wedge the done FSM and lose the hmac_done interrupt
findings.description: In fragment hmac__always_comb__line_149__001, lines 154-161, a reg_hash_stop command in DoneAwaitCmd always moves the FSM to DoneAwaitMessageComplete. However, DoneAwaitMessageComplete only exits on a future digest_on_blk pulse (lines 172-176). There is no handling for the cases where the SHA block is already idle when stop is issued, or where digest_on_blk is asserted in the same cycle as reg_hash_stop and is therefore missed during the state transition. In those cases, the FSM can remain stuck in DoneAwaitMessageComplete waiting for a pulse that may never recur, so hash_done_event is never generated and the interrupt instance in lines 429-440 never sees completion.
findings.security_impact: A malicious or mistimed software command can cause a denial of service on the HMAC completion path by suppressing hmac_done interrupts and potentially blocking correct completion reporting for later operations.

findings.title: cool_down_ct_d is incompletely assigned, creating unintended state retention in done timing logic
findings.description: In fragment hmac__always_comb__line_149__001, lines 149-151 initialize done_state_d and hash_done_event but do not initialize cool_down_ct_d. cool_down_ct_d is only assigned in DoneAwaitCmd (line 155) and in the cool_down_ct_q < 8'd127 sub-branch of DoneAwaitHashComplete (lines 182-185). In DoneAwaitHashDone, DoneAwaitMessageComplete, and other DoneAwaitHashComplete paths, cool_down_ct_d retains its previous value. Since cool_down_ct_q is always clocked from cool_down_ct_d in lines 205-208, this creates unintended stored behavior for the cooldown next-state path and can lead to simulation/synthesis mismatch or incorrect cooldown timing for hash_done_event generation.
findings.security_impact: Unpredictable or stale cooldown timing can cause premature, delayed, or missing completion indication, which may let software act on an incorrect hash-completion state or be denied service by broken interrupt timing.

findings.title: wipe_secret write enable is inverted, so only error transactions trigger secret-wipe side effects
findings.description: In fragment hmac_reg_top__continuous_region__declarations_or_instances__016 (hmac_reg_top.sv around lines 2126-2128), `wipe_secret_we` is assigned as `addr_hit[8] && reg_we && reg_error`, while the surrounding writable registers all use `!reg_error`. In fragment hmac_reg_top__continuous_region__declarations_or_instances__002, `reg_error` is defined as `addrmiss | wr_err | intg_err`, and the `u_wipe_secret` instance consumes this enable via `.we(wipe_secret_we)`. Concrete RTL behavior: a normal, error-free software write to the wipe_secret register will not assert `we` and therefore will not perform the intended wipe; conversely, a transaction that has already been classified as erroneous (including integrity/checking errors) will assert `wipe_secret_we` and still drive `reg2hw.wipe_secret.q/qe`. This means the design commits a state-changing control action on a transaction that the bus reports as failed. Because `wipe_secret_wd` is taken directly from `reg_wdata`, even corrupted or malformed write data can be consumed when `intg_err`/`wr_err` is set.
findings.security_impact: A fault attacker or malicious bus master that can induce write/integrity errors can trigger secret-wipe behavior despite the access being erroneous, causing denial of service and violating the security expectation that integrity-failed transactions must not have architectural side effects.

description: Missing invalid_config_atstart in err_code priority case

findings.title: SHA-384 digest registers expose the full 512-bit internal state
findings.description: In hmac.sv L239-285 (fragment hmac__always_comb__assign_digest_reg__001), the SHA2_384 and SHA2_512 cases are treated identically in the HW->SW digest mapping: when `digest_size_started_q` is `SHA2_384` or `SHA2_512`, the loop writes `hw2reg.digest[2*i]` and `hw2reg.digest[2*i+1]` for all `i = 0..7`. That exposes all 16 32-bit digest CSRs (512 bits) even for SHA-384, which should only return 12 words (384 bits). The extra words leak the truncated-away portion of the final chaining state, so the externally visible result is not a true SHA-384 digest.
findings.security_impact: Software or an attacker with register read access can recover the hidden 128 bits of SHA-384 internal state. This breaks the expected SHA-384 truncation boundary, can enable state-continuation/length-extension style misuse in plain SHA-384 mode, and causes cryptographic non-compliance.

findings.title: TL-UL integrity error output is discarded, weakening or breaking register-bus integrity handling
findings.description: In hmac_reg_top.sv around L141-L162 (fragment hmac_reg_top__continuous_region__declarations_or_instances__002), the register adapter instance `u_reg_if` leaves `.intg_error_o()` unconnected, while `reg_error` is later formed as `addrmiss | wr_err | intg_err`. This explicitly drops the adapter's integrity fault indication instead of propagating it. If `intg_err` was meant to come from `intg_error_o`, this is also a wiring bug that can leave `reg_error` dependent on an undriven/miswired signal. The same instance sets `.EnableDataIntgGen(0)`, further reducing end-to-end integrity protection on this interface.
findings.security_impact: Corrupted or maliciously tampered register transactions may not be detected and reported correctly. In the miswire case, integrity error handling can become undefined, potentially causing silent acceptance of bad bus data or unpredictable fault signaling.

findings.title: Invalid state selector causes self-referential next-state logic for AES-128/192
findings.description: In aes_cipher_core.sv lines 247-255, the `state_mux` default branch assigns `state_d = (key_len_i == AES_256) ? prd_clearing_state_i : state_d;` (line 253). For AES-128 and AES-192, any invalid `state_sel` value therefore makes `state_d` depend on itself instead of forcing a safe value. In hardware this is a strong bug candidate for latch/combinational-feedback behavior, or at minimum a stale-value hold of the previous next-state. Because the state register writes `state_q <= state_d` when `state_we == SP2V_HIGH` (lines 257-263), a transient/glitched/invalid selector can cause old internal AES state to be re-captured rather than cleared. Fragment lines 634-714 only report bad selectors via `mux_sel_err`; they do not sanitize the datapath in the bad cycle, so the unsafe state can be captured before the control FSM locks up and alerts.
findings.security_impact: A fault injection or selector corruption can bypass intended safe clearing/zeroization behavior for AES-128/192, preserving or reloading sensitive intermediate/final AES state. This can leak cryptographic state or enable incorrect-operation attacks before the alert path reacts.

description: Key-clear muxes route to key_expand_out instead of prd_clearing_key_i

findings.title: CLEAR selectors for key registers write key-schedule output instead of clearing data
findings.description: In aes_cipher_core.sv, the explicit clear cases in both key muxes select `key_expand_out` rather than the dedicated clearing input: `KEY_FULL_CLEAR: key_full_d = key_expand_out;` in fragment `aes_cipher_core__always_comb__key_full_mux__001` (lines 438-446) and `KEY_DEC_CLEAR: key_dec_d = key_expand_out;` in fragment `aes_cipher_core__always_comb__key_dec_mux__001` (lines 459-465). The decryption-key register then latches `key_dec_d` when `key_dec_we` is asserted in fragment `aes_cipher_core__always_ff__key_dec_reg__001` (lines 467-473). This means a commanded CLEAR operation does not load `prd_clearing_key_i`; it reuses the normal key-expansion datapath, so the post-clear contents can remain a deterministic function of the existing secret key/state instead of being scrubbed. The fact that the default cases already use `prd_clearing_key_i` makes the explicit CLEAR mapping especially inconsistent and strongly suggests a functional zeroization bug.
findings.security_impact: Key material may survive a zeroization/clear request, leaving secret-dependent values resident in internal registers and potentially observable through later operations, scan/debug exposure, or side-channel analysis.

findings.title: Replicated sparse-selector fault can be masked by OR-combine before downstream validation
findings.description: The selector combiner in fragment `aes_cipher_control__always_comb__combine_sparse_signals__001` (lines 311-339) first ORs all replicated sparse-encoded selector copies into a single value (`state_sel_o`, `add_rk_sel_o`, `key_full_sel_o`, `key_dec_sel_o`, `key_words_sel_o`, `round_key_sel_o`) and only separately raises `mr_err` if any replica differs. In fragment `aes_cipher_core__continuous_region__declarations_or_instances__010` (lines 634-714), the downstream error path `mux_sel_err` is built only from `aes_sel_buf_chk` results on the already-combined selectors (`state_sel_err | add_rk_sel_err | key_full_sel_err | key_dec_sel_err | key_words_sel_err | round_key_sel_err`). A fault that corrupts one replica to 0 or another bit-subset can leave the OR-combined selector equal to the original valid value, so the downstream selector checker will not fire; only `mr_err` detects the disagreement. As shown, that redundancy violation is not part of the `mux_sel_err` aggregation, creating a fault-detection gap.
findings.security_impact: An attacker using fault injection may be able to defeat the replicated-selector hardening and steer internal AES control decisions without triggering the normal mux-selector alert path.

findings.title: Common-mode corruption of sparse mux selectors can bypass both integrity checks
findings.description: In `aes_cipher_control.sv` L311-339 (`combine_sparse_signals`), the redundant selector copies are only checked for equality with each other after being OR-combined. If all `mr_*` copies are identically corrupted to the same different *valid* sparse code, `mr_err` stays `0` because every copy still matches. In `aes_cipher_core.sv` L634-714, `aes_sel_buf_chk` only validates that the code is a member of the allowed sparse set; it does not verify that the selector is the intended value for the current operation. As a result, an attacker or fault can change `state_sel`, `add_rk_sel`, `key_*_sel`, or `round_key_sel` to another valid selector without triggering `mr_err` or `mux_sel_err`. This is a real protection gap on security-critical AES control signals.
findings.security_impact: A fault-injection attacker can redirect internal AES muxes to the wrong state/key/round-key path without an alert, potentially skipping/altering rounds or using wrong key material and enabling differential fault analysis or other cryptographic attacks.

findings.title: `KEY_WORDS_2345` is accepted even when AES-192 support is disabled, causing silent zeroization instead of an error
findings.description: In `aes_cipher_core.sv` L516-535, the `key_words_mux` handles `KEY_WORDS_2345` as `key_words[s] = AES192Enable ? key_full_q[s][5:2] : '0;`. When `AES192Enable` is `0`, this selector does not raise an error; it silently drives zero key words. However, in `aes_cipher_core.sv` L634-714, `u_aes_key_words_sel_buf_chk` still validates `key_words_sel` only against the generic selector encoding set, so `KEY_WORDS_2345` remains an accepted selector value and `key_words_sel_err`/`mux_sel_err` do not assert. Therefore, a control bug or fault that selects `KEY_WORDS_2345` in a non-AES-192 build produces incorrect round-key data with no alert.
findings.security_impact: An attacker can induce faulty AES output by forcing a selector value that is considered valid by the checker but maps to zero key material in this configuration, which can support fault-analysis attacks or silent cryptographic corruption.

description: iv_sel rail OR-merge + iv_we un-gated during CTR
Invalid-stage key leak: exposes raw key_state_q

findings.title: key_state_d is never committed to key_state_q, so key updates and wipes do not actually change the stored key data
findings.description: In keymgr_ctrl__always_comb__line_363__001 (source lines 363-418), all key mutations are computed into key_state_d for Random/Root/KMAC/Wipe updates. However, in keymgr_ctrl__always_ff__line_304__001 (source lines 304-318), the sequential update logic only writes key_state_ecc_q inside the non-reset branch; there is no assignment that updates key_state_q from key_state_d. The ECC checker in keymgr_ctrl__generate_for__gen_ecc_loop_cdi__001 (source lines 321-334) then validates {key_state_ecc_q, key_state_q}. Concretely, after reset, key_state_q stays at its reset value while ECC bits track the new candidate state, so root-key loads, KMAC updates, random initialization, and wipe requests do not change the actual stored key words. This also creates a persistent data/ECC mismatch after any nonzero update.
findings.security_impact: High-risk zeroization failure and stale/predictable key use: a wipe request may leave old key material in storage, and subsequent operations may use stale or all-zero key data while ECC simultaneously reports faults, enabling denial of service or incorrect cryptographic behavior.

findings.title: Likely wrong entropy_i index in KeyUpdateRandom causes incorrect/out-of-range entropy selection
findings.description: In keymgr_ctrl__always_comb__line_363__001, the KeyUpdateRandom path (around source lines 371-376) writes key_state_d[i][j][cnt[EntropyRndWidth-1:0]] = entropy_i[i], using the CDI index i to select entropy. In the same block, the wipe path (around source lines 409-411) uses entropy_i[j], implying entropy_i is share-indexed. If entropy_i is in fact per-share entropy, the random-load path is indexing the wrong dimension: CDIs beyond the number of shares will read invalid/out-of-range entropy, and even in-range cases the wrong entropy source is used for key preloading. That breaks the intended random initialization of masked key shares before the Root update.
findings.security_impact: Incorrect entropy selection can corrupt derived keys and, if masking assumptions are violated, weaken side-channel resistance or cause deterministic/invalid internal key state.

description: Data-enable FSM: illegal encoding silently redirected

findings.title: Key state register is never updated after reset
findings.description: In keymgr_ctrl.sv L304-318, the sequential always_ff block updates only key_state_ecc_q in the non-reset path and never assigns key_state_q <= key_state_d. However, L363-418 computes key_state_d for all key update operations (random load, root key load, KMAC update, and wipe). As written, key_state_q remains stuck at its reset value after reset deassertion, so none of the intended key state transitions ever take effect. This also creates a data/ECC mismatch risk because ECC is re-encoded from the new key_state_ecc_words_d while the underlying key_state_q data is unchanged, which can trigger persistent integrity errors.
findings.security_impact: The key manager can operate on stale or all-zero key material instead of the intended secret state, causing predictable/incorrect derived keys or denial of service through continuous ECC faults. This can break the security guarantees of key generation, advance, disable, and wipe flows.

description: ECC updated without key_state_q -> stale data -> false ecc_errs

findings.title: Key state register is not updated after reset, leaving key material stale/zero and desynchronizing ECC
findings.description: In keymgr_ctrl__always_ff__line_304__001 (source lines 304-318), `key_state_q` is written only in the reset branch (`key_state_q <= '0;`) and there is no non-reset assignment that captures `key_state_d` into `key_state_q`. At the same time, keymgr_ctrl__always_comb__line_363__001 (source lines 363-418) computes `key_state_d` for all key update paths (`KeyUpdateRandom`, `KeyUpdateRoot`, `KeyUpdateKmac`, `KeyUpdateWipe`), so the design clearly expects the key state to change. Instead, the sequential block updates only `key_state_ecc_q` from `key_state_ecc_words_d`. This means attempted key updates may never reach `key_state_q`, leaving the live key state stuck at reset or stale values. The issue is made visible in keymgr_ctrl__generate_for__gen_ecc_loop_cdi__001 (source lines 321-334), where ECC is checked against `{key_state_ecc_q, key_state_q}`: after an attempted update, ECC can correspond to the new value while `key_state_q` still contains the old/zero value, causing persistent ECC mismatch/faults.
findings.security_impact: This can cause denial of service through continuous ECC fault detection and can also make the key manager operate on stale or all-zero/predictable key state instead of the intended secret state.

findings.title: TX watermark threshold shift is width-truncated, disabling most TX watermark interrupts
findings.description: In `uart_core.sv` lines 319-321 (`uart_core__always_comb__line_313__001`), the threshold is computed as `tx_watermark_thresh = 1'b1 << uart_fifo_txilvl;`. In SystemVerilog, the result width of a shift expression is the width of the left operand, so this expression is only 1 bit wide. For any `uart_fifo_txilvl > 0`, the shifted value is truncated to `1'b0` before being assigned to `tx_watermark_thresh`. As a result, for non-saturated TX watermark levels the computed threshold becomes 0, and `event_tx_watermark = tx_fifo_depth < tx_watermark_thresh;` on line 321 can never assert. This broken event is then wired into the TX watermark interrupt generator in lines 406-417 (`intr_hw_tx_watermark`), so software-programmed TX watermark interrupt levels can silently stop working for most settings.
findings.security_impact: An attacker or faulty software that relies on TX watermark interrupts can cause interrupt-driven transmit handling to stall or hang, creating a denial-of-service condition or suppressing expected UART activity notifications.

description: Break FSM re-arms on single rx_in high

findings.title: line_loopback mode forces RX input to constant idle instead of a looped-back signal
findings.description: In fragment uart_core__continuous_region__declarations_or_instances__004, source lines 262-264, `rx_in` is selected as `sys_loopback ? tx_out : line_loopback ? 1'b1 : rx_in_mx;`. When `line_loopback` is asserted, the receiver input is hard-wired to `1'b1` (idle) rather than any transmitted or pad-observed serial data. Concrete RTL behavior: in line-loopback mode the RX path can never see start bits, data bits, parity errors, framing errors, or break conditions, because `uart_rx.rx` is permanently high. This makes the line-loopback mode non-functional and also affects break handling in fragment uart_core__always_ff__line_123__001 (lines 123-140), since `break_st_q` uses `rx_in` and will observe a forced-idle line under line loopback.
findings.security_impact: Primarily a functional/availability issue: firmware self-test or diagnostic code that relies on line-loopback can be bypassed or falsely pass/fail because the receiver never observes actual serial activity. This can hide UART path faults and disable expected monitoring in loopback mode.
